launch_app.description: Launch an installed app. On VIDAA sets url is the short store name with urlType 37 (netflix, youtube, amazon, disneyplus, plex); on Android-TV-based sets url is the Android package name and urlType is 0. Both forms, with names, come from the applist reply.

name.description: Display name exactly as applist reports it, e.g. 'Netflix'.

url.description: VIDAA short name ('netflix') or Android package name ('com.netflix.ninja'); matches the urlType the set expects.

press_back.description: Back one screen. The wire spelling is KEY_RETURNS.

press_fast_forward.description: Fast-forward. The wire spelling is KEY_FORWARDS.

press_power.description: Power toggle (standby<->on). The broker is down while the TV is off, so this only ever turns a TV OFF over MQTT — power on is WoL.

press_rewind.description: Rewind. The wire spelling is KEY_BACK — NOT KEY_REWIND; do not confuse it with KEY_RETURNS (the Back button).

set_source.description: Switch input by numeric id. Ids are the fixed table 0 TV, 1 AV, 2 Component, 3-6 HDMI 1-4; sourcelist reports which of them the set actually has.

sourceid.description: Input id as a decimal string.

set_volume.description: Set absolute volume, 0-100. The payload is the bare decimal level as a string, NOT JSON.

volume.description: Absolute volume level; rendered into the payload as the bare decimal string.

match.description: Keep only renderers whose fetched descriptor has manufacturer "Hisense" — or, stronger, a modelDescription containing vidaa_support=1 or a transport_protocol key. Older firmware reports vidaa_support=0 while still speaking the protocol, so transport_protocol (a VIDAA-specific key unrelated UPnP renderers never publish) must also count as a match.
match.rule: manufacturer == 'Hisense' OR modelDescription contains 'vidaa_support=1' OR modelDescription contains 'transport_protocol='

parse.example:
<root xmlns="urn:schemas-upnp-org:device-1-0">
  <device>
    <deviceType>urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:MediaRenderer:1</deviceType>
    <friendlyName>Living Room TV</friendlyName>
    <manufacturer>Hisense</manufacturer>
    <modelName>Renderer</modelName>
    <modelDescription>mac=38D65D000000
macEthernet=38D65D000000
macWifi=38D65D000001
brand=his
vidaa_support=1
transport_protocol=3290</modelDescription>
  </device>
</root>
parse_rules: The descriptor is served on port 38400 (some VIDAA OS versions use 18400; try both, 38400 first), at path /MediaServer/rendererdevicedesc.xml.
modelDescription is not prose but newline-separated key=value pairs: mac, macWifi, macEthernet, brand, vidaa_support, transport_protocol. Parse it as a map, not as text.
modelName is often literally 'Renderer' — model identity comes from modelDescription.brand and friendlyName, not modelName.
macEthernet and macWifi are reported separately; Wake-on-LAN must target whichever interface the TV actually uses, and the descriptor does not say which.

device.name: Hisense VIDAA TV (remoteapp MQTT)
device.notes: Hisense TVs run an on-device MQTT broker on TCP port 36669 (mosquitto 1.4.2 on the oldest observed firmware) which exists to serve the official RemoteNow and VIDAA mobile apps. All control is publish/subscribe: commands go to /remoteapp/tv/{service}/{client_id}/actions/{action} and answers come back on /remoteapp/mobile/{client_id}/... or on broadcast topics under /remoteapp/mobile/broadcast/. The service vocabulary is remote_service (sendkey), ui_service (state, sources, apps, pairing) and platform_service (volume, tokens). Despite the brief's expectation of a distinct older port: no source documents a listener on 36668 — the "older remoteapp protocol" is the same broker on the same 36669 without TLS and with the static hisenseservice/multimqttservice login, not a different port. Discovery is SSDP/DLNA (the TV is a UPnP MediaRenderer) plus a Hisense-specific UDP broadcast on port 36671; identity comes from the UPnP device descriptor on port 38400 (18400 on some VIDAA versions). There is no way to power these TVs on over this protocol — the broker is down in standby, so wake is Wake-on-LAN to the TV's MAC.

openness.notes: Hisense publishes nothing about this interface. Everything here was recovered by the community from packet captures, the RemoteNow and VIDAA Android APKs (libmqttcrypt.so in particular), and live probing — Krazy998/mqtt-hisensetv documented the broker and topic vocabulary in 2019, newAM/hisensetv and sehaas/ha_hisense_tv productised the static and cert generations, and warrenrees/pyvidaa reverse-engineered the dynamic credential algorithm from the VIDAA app's native library and verified it end-to-end on a live set (field notes dated 2026-08-04). The VIDAA app itself is Baidu-packed and certificate-pinned, which is why the modern generation took until 2024-2026 to document.

issued_to_client: accesstoken + refreshtoken (modern firmware only, via the tokenissuance topic; accesstoken becomes the MQTT password)
credentials.notes: THE CERT-PROVISIONING GAP: on VIDAA-era firmware the broker demands mutual TLS, and the client certificate is NOT provisioned by any pairing flow — the TV has no protocol for enrolling a new certificate. Every working client presents the same cert baked into the official app: CN=VidaaAppAndroidV01, issued by the private RemoteCA root, extracted from the VIDAA APK's PKCS#12 keystore (assets/client_mobile_android.p12, or res/3R.p12 under newer obfuscated resource names; store password 186e990688070325a1c4b0ce275d2388, recovered from libmqttcrypt.so). RemoteNow-era sets that require certs accept the older rcm_certchain_pem.cer / rcm_pem_privkey.pkcs8 pair circulated in d3nd3/Hisense-mqtt-keyfiles. A clean-room client therefore cannot complete modern pairing without redistributing Hisense's key material or asking the user to extract it — that, not the topic vocabulary, is the barrier to a fully open implementation.
stored_on_device: List of authorized client ids (the MAC-shaped uuid each paired client chose)
Issued access/refresh tokens per paired client (modern firmware)
RemoteCA private root material guarding the broker (never leaves the TV)

factory_reset.effect: Clears network credentials, the VIDAA/Hisense account link, the paired-client list (every authorized client id must re-pair), installed-app sign-ins and all settings; the TV returns to first-run setup.

procedures.indicator: TV reboots into the first-run wizard.
procedures.name: Menu factory reset (VIDAA)

steps.action: Settings > Support > Reset to Factory Default (on Android-TV-based Hisense sets: Settings > Device Preferences > Reset).
steps.notes: Menu paths vary by OS generation and region; both spellings are reported. No hardware pinhole reset is documented for these sets.

methods.description: Guided first-run setup on the TV itself: language, network selection, passphrase entry on the on-screen keyboard, optional VIDAA/Hisense account link. The account gates app-store features, not the local broker.

steps.action: Power on the TV and follow the on-screen setup with the remote.
Select the WiFi network (or plug in Ethernet) and enter the passphrase on the TV itself.
Confirm the broker is reachable from the LAN.
steps.expect: Retained state message with a statetype field arrives immediately on subscribe (the state topic is retained).

steps.action: Pair the client id: trigger the on-screen PIN, then publish the 4-digit code.
steps.expect: Reply {"result": 1} on /remoteapp/mobile/{client_id}/ui_service/data/authenticationcode; on modern firmware, a tokenissuance message follows.

steps.action: Read the 4-digit PIN from the TV screen and type it into the client within about 60 seconds.

setup.notes: Two unrelated things both called "setup" here. Network onboarding is entirely on the TV's own screen (Settings > Network); there is no app-driven provisioning protocol to reimplement. CLIENT pairing is the real gate and it is part of the MQTT protocol itself: an unpaired client can connect and subscribe to broadcast topics, but commands are ignored until the client id has been authorized by a PIN shown on the TV screen. The pairing exchange is documented step by step in remoteapp_common.pairing. On modern (VIDAA-app-era) firmware pairing additionally requires the mutual-TLS client certificate, which the TV never issues — it must be extracted from the official app, the cert-provisioning gap recorded in credentials.notes below.

rejoin.notes: Settings > Network > (select the network) re-runs only the network step. Paired clients survive; a factory reset is never needed just to change routers.

characteristics: Model the original Krazy998/mqtt-hisensetv documentation was written against: plain or self-signed-TLS broker, static hisenseservice/multimqttservice login, no client certificate, mosquitto 1.4.2.
variants.name: Hisense 75P7 (2019, VIDAA U 2.5 era)

characteristics: Reported by newAM/hisensetv to have no TLS at all on 36669 — plain MQTT with the static login.
variants.name: Hisense H43A6250UK

characteristics: sehaas/ha_hisense_tv's reference hardware: mandatory client certificates with the static login; gettvstate returns no state but doubles as the pairing trigger.
variants.name: Hisense A71 series

characteristics: Rejects the static login outright ('Connection refused: Identifier rejected'); pairs only with the VIDAA app. Dynamic timestamp-derived credentials required (Krazy998 issue #14).
variants.name: Hisense 55U7KQ (2023, VIDAA-app-only)

characteristics: pyvidaa's live-probed set (2026-08-04): modern auth verified end to end; gettvstate unanswered on this firmware — state arrives only as unsolicited broadcast; standby reported as statetype fake_sleep_0.
variants.name: Hisense 32A35HUV (firmware V0002.09.01O.P0814, MTK9602)

entities.name: Power
entities.notes: Toggle. Turning the TV ON from standby is Wake-on-LAN, not this button — the broker is down while off.

entities.name: Volume
entities.notes: State arrives as {"volume_type": 0, "volume_value": N}; read volume_value.

entities.name: Input
entities.notes: Current input: read statetype from the state topic — "sourceswitch" carries sourceid directly; "livetv" is the tuner (sourceid "0"); anything else (remote_launcher, remote_setting) is an app or menu, i.e. no input selected. Filter the static option list against the sourcelist reply: a set with three HDMIs still accepts the ids, but only offers what sourcelist reported.

entities.name: TV State
entities.notes: The statetype field (fake_sleep_0 = standby; fake_sleep_1 = waking, NOT asleep; remote_launcher = home; livetv/sourceswitch carry channel/source detail).

open_questions: No source documents any listener on port 36668; treated here as a premise error until a capture says otherwise.
Whether the broker really isolates one client's topics from another is unconfirmed — the one isolation experiment predates the discovery that wildcard subscriptions work, and has not been repeated.
changechannel exists but takes an opaque channel_param string read from livetv state; there is no documented way to tune to channel N without first learning that string from the TV.
evidence.provenance: This project has NOT probed a Hisense TV. Every fact above is "reported" from the cited community sources, of which the strongest is pyvidaa's 2026-08-04 field-notes section: an explicitly tagged live/native/ inferred record against a 32A35HUV_0002 (firmware V0002.09.01O.P0814), including byte-for-byte reproduction of the modern credential algorithm and a corrected (wildcards work) topic surface. The 2019 static-login vocabulary rests on Krazy998's original capture against a 75P7.

http_endpoints.description: The DLNA/UPnP MediaRenderer descriptor, on port 38400 (18400 on some VIDAA OS versions — try both, 38400 first; the SSDP LOCATION header says which). friendlyName is the user-facing name; modelName is often literally "Renderer"; the identity lives in modelDescription, a newline-separated key=value map (mac, macWifi, macEthernet, brand, vidaa_support, transport_protocol). This is the ONLY HTTP surface documented on these TVs — every control path is MQTT.
http_endpoints.name: UPnP Device Descriptor

    <manufacturer>Hisense</manufacturer>

macEthernet=38D65D000000

mqtt_topics.description: One remote key press. Payload is the bare key name from remoteapp_common.key_vocabulary (e.g. KEY_POWER) — not JSON.
mqtt_topics.name: Send Key

mqtt_topics.description: Ask for the current state object (and, on unpaired clients, trigger the PIN dialog). Empty payload. NOT answered on all firmware — the pyvidaa-probed set never replies; treat the retained broadcast state topic as authoritative and this as a poke.
mqtt_topics.name: Get TV State

mqtt_topics.description: Ask for the input list; the reply arrives on this client's ui_service/data/sourcelist as a JSON array of {sourceid, sourcename, displayname, is_signal, is_lock, hotel_mode}. Empty payload.
mqtt_topics.name: Get Source List

mqtt_topics.description: Switch input. Payload {"sourceid": "3"}; sourceid alone is sufficient (sourcename optional — and spell it without the space, "HDMI1", if sent; the 2019 docs note "HDMI 1" with a space errors). Ids: 0 TV, 1 AV, 2 Component, 3-6 HDMI 1-4.
mqtt_topics.name: Change Source

fields.description: Input id as a decimal string.
fields.name: sourceid

mqtt_topics.description: Launch an installed app. VIDAA payload: {"name": "Netflix", "urlType": 37, "storeType": 0, "url": "netflix"} — url is the short store name; urlType 37 means exactly that. Android-TV-based sets instead take the Android package name in url with urlType 0 (newAM's table: com.netflix.ninja, com.google.android.youtube.tv, com.amazon.amazonvideo.livingroom, com.disney.disneyplus, ...). Names for either form come from the applist reply.
mqtt_topics.name: Launch App

mqtt_topics.description: Ask for installed apps; the reply (name, appId, url per app) arrives on this client's ui_service/data/applist. Empty payload.
mqtt_topics.name: Get App List

mqtt_topics.description: Tune to a specific channel. Payload {"channel_param": "<opaque>"} — the string is learned from the livetv state object's channel_param field (or captured while the official app sets a favourite); there is no documented way to construct it from a channel number. Treated as VIDAA-era; hypothesis-grade for general use.
mqtt_topics.name: Change Channel

mqtt_topics.description: Ask for volume; reply {"volume_type": 0, "volume_value": N} on this client's platform_service/data/volume (or the broadcast volumechange topic). Empty payload.
mqtt_topics.name: Get Volume

mqtt_topics.description: Set absolute volume. Payload is the bare decimal level 0-100 as a string, not JSON.
mqtt_topics.name: Change Volume

mqtt_topics.description: Modern pairing step 1: payload {"app_version": 2, "connect_result": 0, "device_type": "Mobile App"} puts the PIN dialog on the TV screen.
mqtt_topics.name: VIDAA App Connect (pairing trigger)

mqtt_topics.description: Pairing step 2: payload {"authNum": "XXXX"} with the 4-digit PIN on screen. Success replies {"result": 1} on this client's ui_service/data/authenticationcode.
mqtt_topics.name: Send Authentication Code

mqtt_topics.description: Modern pairing step 3 and every later refresh: payload {"refreshtoken": ""} to mint the first pair, {"refreshtoken": "<saved>"} to rotate. Replies on this client's platform_service/data/tokenissuance.
mqtt_topics.name: Get/Refresh Token

mqtt_topics.description: THE state channel: retained JSON object keyed by statetype (fake_sleep_0/1, remote_launcher, remote_setting, sourceswitch, livetv — see remoteapp_common.state_vocabulary). livetv carries channel_name/channel_num/channel_param and, on older firmware, EPG fields; sourceswitch carries sourceid/sourcename/displayname.
mqtt_topics.name: TV State Broadcast

mqtt_topics.description: Volume changes as the TV sees them (remote included): {"volume_type": 0, "volume_value": N}.
mqtt_topics.name: Volume Broadcast

mqtt_topics.description: Reply to the sourcelist action: JSON array of {sourceid, sourcename, displayname, is_signal, is_lock, hotel_mode}.
mqtt_topics.name: Source List Reply

mqtt_topics.description: Reply to the applist action: JSON array with name, appId and url per installed app — the values launchapp takes.
mqtt_topics.name: App List Reply

mqtt_topics.description: Empty-payload push meaning the PIN dialog is on screen (modern pairing); the sibling topics authenticationcodetoast/authenticationcodeclose track its lifecycle.
mqtt_topics.name: PIN Dialog Notification

mqtt_topics.description: Access/refresh tokens after pairing or refresh: {accesstoken, accesstoken_time, accesstoken_duration_day, refreshtoken, refreshtoken_time, refreshtoken_duration_day}.
mqtt_topics.name: Token Issuance

authentication.after_pairing: Once paired, modern firmware issues tokens: the accesstoken becomes the MQTT password (same client_id and username) until it expires (accesstoken_duration_day, observed 2-30 days), after which the client reconnects once with the OLD credential algorithm to publish {"refreshtoken": "<saved>"} to /remoteapp/tv/platform_service/{client_id}/data/gettoken and reads a fresh pair from /remoteapp/mobile/{client_id}/platform_service/data/tokenissuance. The refresh token itself lasts refreshtoken_duration_day (observed 30-365) — miss that window and the client must re-pair with a PIN.

generations.client_id: Arbitrary; convention is the client's own MAC with $normal appended (newAM), or a plain name like 'HomeAssistant'. Reusing a client id drops the older session, so do not share ids between integrations.
generations.name: static

generations.algorithm: All MD5 hex digests uppercase. Let PATTERN = "38D65DC30F45109A369A86FCE866A85B", uuid = the client's chosen MAC-shaped identifier (colon-separated, any case as minted), ts = current unix time in seconds, and crosssum(ts) = sum of the decimal digits of ts. Then: client_id = uuid + "$his$" + md5(PATTERN + "$" + uuid)[:6] + "_vidaacommon_001"; username = "his$" + ts; password = md5(ts + "$" + md5("his" + (crosssum(ts) % 10) + "h*i&s%e!r^v0i1c9")[:6]).
generations.applies: VIDAA-app-era firmware before the modern tweak (pyvidaa: 3000 <= transport_protocol < 3290; e.g. the 2023 A6K/55U8KQ captures)
generations.name: legacy_dynamic
generations.validity: The TV checks the timestamp in the username, so a generated login works only for roughly +/-4 hours. Passwords carry no TV-specific material — one capture worked on a second TV (issue #14), which is a security note as much as an implementation one.

generations.algorithm: Identical to legacy_dynamic with two changes: the password suffix is "h!i@s#$v%i^d&a*a" instead of "h*i&s%e!r^v0i1c9", and the username's timestamp is obfuscated — username = "his$" + (ts XOR 0x569814772b03a968). pyvidaa reproduces all three values byte-for-byte against the app on a live set (2026-08-04); its worked example: uuid 56:b8:88:4e:f7:19, ts 1766974704 → client_id 56:b8:88:4e:f7:19$his$256DBF_vidaacommon_001, username his$6239759786168176024, password C3BA44782E18ABF4892AC44D79A622D2.
generations.applies: Current VIDAA firmware (pyvidaa: transport_protocol >= 3290); requires the mtls generation above
generations.name: modern_dynamic
generations.notes: The uuid is minted by the CLIENT, not read from hardware — the app generates a fresh MAC-shaped value on every reinstall, and the client id carries both the uuid and md5(PATTERN$uuid)[:6], so the check is self-consistent. Any stable, self-consistent identifier is believed acceptable (pyvidaa: inferred, not verified). The app opens a second connection with operation "vidaavoice" instead of "vidaacommon"; one connection suffices for control. A _002 client-id suffix exists in the binary but only _001 has been observed on the wire.

broker.keepalive_notes: These TVs vanish from the network in standby without closing the session, so keepalive is what bounds how long a dead session looks alive: paho gives up at roughly 1.5x. The old 60s default meant ~90s before a powered-off TV was noticed.
broker.port_36668_note: No source documents a listener on 36668. Older models run the SAME broker on 36669 with no TLS and the static login (newAM's --no-ssl flag exists for exactly those sets). If a scan shows 36668 open on some set, its role is unestablished — capture it before writing it down.

key_vocabulary.notes: Wire spellings are the VIDAA APK's: back is KEY_RETURNS and rewind is KEY_BACK, the two most surprising names in the table. KEY_POWER is a toggle — there is no separate power-on key, and no network power-on at all (broker is down in standby): power-on is Wake-on-LAN to the TV's MAC, Ethernet far more reliably than WiFi.

modern_generation: Connect over mTLS with dynamic credentials; subscribe to the client's data topics (or /remoteapp/# — see topic_format.wildcards).

TV either pushes an empty message on /remoteapp/mobile/{client_id}/ui_service/data/authentication (PIN now on screen) or answers vidaa_app_connect with {"connect_result": 1} — already authorized, no PIN needed.
User reads the 4-digit PIN; client publishes {"authNum": "XXXX"} to actions/authenticationcode; {"result": 1, "info": ""} confirms.

Publish {"refreshtoken": ""} to /remoteapp/tv/platform_service/{client_id}/data/gettoken and read accesstoken/refreshtoken (+ durations and issue times) from platform_service/data/tokenissuance. Store them — they replace the password from now on (see authentication.after_pairing).
Publish anything to actions/authenticationcodeclose to dismiss the dialog.
static_generation: Connect with the static login; subscribe to /remoteapp/mobile/{client_id}/ui_service/data/authenticationcode.
Publish anything to /remoteapp/tv/ui_service/{client_id}/actions/gettvstate — the request doubles as the pairing trigger; the TV shows a 4-digit PIN.
User reads the PIN; client publishes {"authNum": "XXXX"} to /remoteapp/tv/ui_service/{client_id}/actions/authenticationcode.
Reply {"result": 1} on the authenticationcode data topic means the client id (its uuid) is now authorized. Any other result is a refusal; the PIN dialog times out in about 60 seconds.
pairing.user_visible: The PIN appears as an on-screen dialog without the user touching the TV; the user's only job is reading four digits into the client within the ~60s timeout. TVs may cap the number of paired clients — old pairings are removable in the TV's settings.

state_vocabulary.notes: On the pyvidaa-probed firmware gettvstate is never answered — state arrives only as unsolicited broadcast on /remoteapp/mobile/broadcast/ui_service/state — while the 2019 documentation shows gettvstate producing exactly that state object. A client must therefore treat the broadcast topic as the state channel and gettvstate as, at best, a poke. Volume changes broadcast on /remoteapp/mobile/broadcast/platform_service/actions/volumechange.

statetype.fake_sleep_0: standby (match this exactly — fake_sleep_1 is WAKING, followed by remote_launcher)
statetype.livetv: watching a tuner channel; carries channel_name, channel_num, channel_param, sourceid — and EPG fields (progname, starttime, endtime) on older firmware; NO sourcename/displayname
statetype.sourceswitch: external input; carries sourceid, sourcename, displayname, is_signal

generations.description: No TLS at all. Oldest sets (e.g. H43A6250UK).
generations.name: plain

generations.description: TLS with a self-signed server certificate; clients must disable verification (encryption on, validate off).
generations.name: tls_selfsigned

generations.description: Mutual TLS: the client must present the app-bundled certificate CN=VidaaAppAndroidV01 (issuer CN=RemoteCA) or the RemoteNow-era rcm pair — see device.setup.credentials.notes for the provisioning gap. Server certificate issued by the same private RemoteCA root; CN is 'RemoteCA', so hostname checks always fail and verification stays off even in careful clients.
generations.name: mtls

topic_format.payloads: Payloads are plain JSON, or a bare string where the vocabulary says so: sendkey takes the key name itself ("KEY_POWER"), changevolume takes the bare decimal level ("50"), and several query actions take an empty payload (publish a zero-length message or a single "0" — both are in circulation).
topic_format.subscribe_broadcast: /remoteapp/mobile/broadcast/{service}/... — state all clients share; /remoteapp/mobile/broadcast/ui_service/state is RETAINED, so a fresh subscriber learns the current statetype immediately
topic_format.wildcards: Long believed denied by the broker; a 2026-08-04 live probe found /remoteapp/# granted and delivering (the earlier SUBACK-0x80 claim was a broken calibration). Treat specific subscriptions as the contract and wildcards as a debugging convenience — the belief has flipped once already.

remoteapp_common.transport_gap: The reference app speaks HTTP (GET/POST, empty body) and SOAP today. This device needs an MQTT client with: TLS and client-certificate support, per-connection dynamic credential generation (the MD5/XOR algorithm above), the pairing flow with user-supplied PIN, token storage and scheduled refresh, and JSON-over-MQTT command payloads. None of that maps onto either supported transport, so the `commands` below declare transport: "mqtt" — schema-legal but not yet executable by the reference app. They are written as invocations so that an MQTT transport, once added, can run them unchanged.
